utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, I still can say, not yet good afternoon to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, Case Number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Stewart, I do understand that you would like to address the Chamber at the same time, but before giving you an opportunity to do so, I'd like to ask the Registry and the technicians since we met for the second day the same problems in the morning with the equipment, to start testing a bit earlier, perhaps tomorrow and see whether we could start in time. Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, very briefly, it's this. That after the question of whether Mr. Trbojevic should come back or give his evidence by videolink was raised by the Trial Chamber on Friday, apparently immediate inquiries were made as to relative costs of videolink and his coming back which was clearly regarded as a material consideration although, naturally, it would not be decisive consideration. It's this, Your Honour, that Your Honours have in effect ruled on the matter which Your Honours raised and which was briefly discussed in court on Friday in the way that the Defence wished. So clearly I have no particular problem with that, Your Honour. It's just that that is a decision among the factors as the ones I've mentioned and there are other factors and I would invite the Trial Chamber at some convenient point to express very clearly for the benefit of the Defence and the public, indeed, and including in that the information as to the relative costs because -- so these are all material considerations, it is also important in this matter and for guidance in the future for such matters for the Defence and the parties generally to understand as clearly as possible what the Trial Chamber's approach has been in reaching that decision in relation to Mr. Trbojevic, and how the relative factors including the question of cost are balanced in relation to such an issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll consider the matter and we'll see whether this is something suitable for general considerations or whether we would deal with it at a case-by-case basis including, of course, all relevant circumstances of which costs is one. Then -- yes, Mr. Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom. Mr. Stewart, could you give us any idea of how much time you would still need for further cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I was going to estimate about a target and a hopeful, realistic target of finishing cross-examination by the second break. Clearly that might be subject to the appropriate adjustment in the light of the fact that it's just after 25 to 10.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Under the 60 per cent guidance, which the Chamber is not very much inclined to apply at this moment, there would be another half an hour. But like I said, the Chamber in view of the circumstances is not very much inclined to stick to that guidance. On the other hand, until the second break would take us two and a half more hours. You are invited to see whether it could be a bit shorter and the Chamber will certainly assist you in working as efficiently as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm much obliged for that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say straightaway though, just to inquire and it's appropriate to make this inquiry with the witness here, to speed things along -- Your Honour, I hope the Trial Chamber has received and is aware of the further material which Mr. Kljuic produced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber is aware of the arrival of the material.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I inquire whether the Chamber has had any opportunity whatever of considering that material? Well, has taken the opportunity in considering that material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I received it this morning and we have not had an opportunity yet to go through it. And of course we have no translation at all, but the Chamber will wait and see what the parties will do with it. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have one matter to raise and that is that yesterday, there was a cross-examination on a document, one of the notes of Mr. Kljuic. And for purposes of this record, I think it should be given an exhibit number if it hasn't already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we -- yesterday, cross-examination was about I think Exhibit 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: 14, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken. May I take it that you will tender that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honour, it was item 14 of that batch, wasn't it. And yes, of course, I don't currently remember where we got to in D numbers but Ms. Philpott is always on top of such things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you assign a D number to item 14 of the -- well let's say the first batch of materials that Mr. Kljuic had sent to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will be Defence Exhibit D40.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, the -- so far as the new material is concerned, we received it yesterday afternoon. Your Honour appreciates that it is quite naturally all in Mr. Kljuic's own language. We do have some resources, of course, which enable us to cope with -- in addition to Mr. Krajisnik who is not easy to get hold of in relation to such matters, for obvious reasons -- we do have some resources, but Your Honour, they are necessarily limited and our resources in that area do have other urgent tasks at all times. So Your Honour, we have, we, the team, have conducted a review of this material until sometime in the middle of the night but it's not complete, Your Honour. And Mr. Krajisnik, to whom I have handed the relevant new material in court this morning, has had no opportunity whatever to deal with this matter. Your Honour, it's not quite easy to know where to go here. The -- at the very least, I hope that -- well, I know enough already from what I have been told by Ms. Cmeric to know that a review by Mr. Krajisnik of this material is not just a 15, 20 minute job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's see, let's first continue cross-examination and see whether -- how we will proceed in relation to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, I'm going to have to ask you straightaway about this material. Mr. Kljuic, you do not seem to have included in the previous batch of items or the new batch of items -- I call them that -- of those notes that you referred to in your evidence in September as your having taken in the course of meetings with, for example, Dr. Karadzic and then a number of other people were mentioned. Mr. Kljuic, have you simply left such notes behind you back in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. All the notes that I made at that time were integrated with the material that I sent to you. As I was writing certain chapters, I was giving the attitude towards the future of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the constitutional amendments so that my notes are basically interwoven into these texts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, can I get it clear. Are you saying that there is no material in the form of any notes or memorandums of any sort written by you in 1990, 1991, 1992, in relation to all these political matters, that there are no such notes back in Sarajevo additional to what you have delivered already to this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not as such. They were used for my writing and were then dispensed of.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, that's -- I'm asking you about what is currently physically in existence. Are you saying there is nothing of any possible relevance to your evidence prepared by you back in Sarajevo additionally to what you have already given this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The parts that were already described, no. As for the rest, I don't know whether there's something else within my documentation. Whatever I could find I have brought over with me. However, there are no specific notes concerning these meetings because I integrated them into my book and I have them as sections of my book, but you've said that you're not interested in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I only ask questions, Mr. Kljuic. But you are quite right, my primary interest in the questions is not in chapters of your book as opposed to contemporaneous matters and His Honour Judge Orie made that clear to you back in September. That's the background to it. Mr. Kljuic, is it this that when you have used or -- notes, contemporaneous notes that you had made in 1990, 1991, 1992, when you have used those for a chapter in your book, you have then thrown them away or destroyed them, have you?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were destroyed because the secretaries, once they typed them out, there was no more need for them because this was an enormous amount of documentation containing even copies of newspaper articles. This was basically a documentation centre from which I took only those parts that I was interested in and I dispensed of the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, let's just focus on your own notes that you - forget newspaper articles - your own notes that you told this Tribunal in sent you had made at meetings with Dr. Karadzic and so on. You agree, do you, that -- maybe at the time, but looking back, these were, for better or worse, historic events that you were involved with, weren't they? That's obvious, Mr. Kljuic, isn't it, please?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I've never stated that I made any notes of the talks with Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... please answer my question, Mr. Kljuic. I thought you might simply readily agree. These were historic events, weren't they, that you were involved in?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you are an academic; correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could put it that way. I'm not a member of any academy, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You're writing a book; correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have written several books so far, plays, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You're writing a book that you've told this Tribunal about, aren't you? That's what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you're saying that as you go along, you throw away - please say whether this is right or wrong. You have thrown away your original source material consisting of your own notes from that historic period; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once I've used up my own note for the purposes of my book, that's good enough for me. I get rid of these old papers because they are personal notes and not documents of any significance for others.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Is the answer yes, you have thrown away your own contemporaneous notes of these meetings, for example, with Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because they were transposed into new texts. So I have not torn them up without having used them. I have used them in the parts that I deemed fit and then threw them away because I got rid of a number of other papers dating from that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Have you finished with and therefore thrown away all the notes that you mentioned in September that you took of any meetings at which Mr. -- Dr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, Mr. Koljevic, Mrs. Plavsic and so on were present?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the papers that I have used and copied from were thrown. Other contemporaneous papers from 1990, 1991, 1992 that I have not used for my book, I have brought them over for you to see. Had I known that 13 years later, anyone would inquire of me to show these papers, I would have them now because as it was, I merely considered them my property.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You referred to -- I'm pretty sure you did, refer to a secretary typing up your notes. Is that one stage of the process of your work that your handwritten notes of meetings in that period, 1990 to 1992, were typed up?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only the portions that were deemed significant by me were typed out and are contained in these texts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And was the typed-up version, then, of such notes, also thrown away as you incorporated such material into chapters or draft chapters of your book?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depending on the case. Not necessarily all of them, but I was interested in having them transposed into my book as their final version. Everything else was considered by me to be merely a preparatory version while writing the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Let me go as directly as I can to it, Mr. Kljuic. Apart from the material that you've already supplied to the Tribunal in two batches, do you or might you have back in Bosnia either original notes of yours made in 1990, 1991, or 1992 in relation to these political events or typed-up copies or typed-up versions of such notes? That is if you want the question given to you again, Mr. Kljuic, then I would take it that that is a yes or no question.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no need for repeating.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Is the answer yes or no, please?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There may be some, I'm not sure. I would have to check.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Would you be willing to check as soon as convenient when you return to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And would you be willing, without any expurgation or sifting to supply copies of all that material to this Tribunal, if so requested?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already given two batches of these papers; therefore, there's no reason why I shouldn't give you this one as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I take that as a yes, you would be willing, Mr. Kljuic.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, either now or at some point that's convenient, I do invite the Tribunal to -- to the Trial Chamber to make that request. I'm in Your Honours' hands as to when, of course -- well strictly whether. But I'm inviting that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll consider that. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: If Your Honour is at any point -- may I just say if Your Honour's at any point considering rejecting that request, might I please be given a suitable opportunity at a suitable point of making submissions first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may. We'll consider whether we are inclined or not inclined to give such an order. If we are not inclined to give such an order, we'll giver you an opportunity to make brief submissions on the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm obliged, Your Honour. And I'm sure of course the Trial Chamber would give Mr. Harmon whatever opportunity is suitable for him in whatever circumstances. I wouldn't of course resist that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, I'm now going to turn back to some of the evidence which you've already given in this case. At page, it's 6.100. Your Honour likes the day -- it's Monday, the 27th of September, 2004, you said, it's line 5, "Since after Dayton Accords were signed, Karadzic could not occupy a political position having been eliminated by Americans from political life and that was one of the conditions of the Dayton Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Accords. Mr. Krajisnik became officially the leader of Bosnian Serbs." In what -- you say "officially." In what way did Mr. Krajisnik become officially the leader of the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very simply, he has become a candidate of -- for the president -- to be a become a member of the Presidency. He won the elections after the Dayton Accord and became a member of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What made him the -- officially the leader of the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This position in the Presidency, because in the aftermath of the Dayton Accords, only three members were elected on the Presidency, these were the three representatives of the three ethnic groups, Croats, Serbs and Muslims. Having been elected a member of the Presidency, he officially became a representative of Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Who became, at that point, the president of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. Perhaps Poplasen or Ms. Plavsic, they were presidents after the war, but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I put it to you that it was Mrs. Plavsic that you don't -- well it's at least apparent - you don't recall anything to contradict that, do you?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, undoubtedly, this was an electoral position.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And Mr. Buha became the president of the SDS, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly so. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You said, and this is the next page of that transcript, page 6.101, line 5: "Later, we would get a major confirmation that not all Serbs were in favour of Karadzic and when a referendum for the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina was declared on 22nd of March, 1991, a great number of Serbs, possibly a third, and there would have been even more if the referendum had not been declared on the entire territory, did support the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina." Is that speculation, assessment, or based on some hard facts your one-third, "possibly one-third" remark?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your question is first of all a bit confusing. There are several inaccuracies in it. The referendum for the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina was the 29th of February and the 22nd of March.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Not the 22nd of March. Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So the information contained in my testimony is as follows: You have to know that the structure of the population deferred from the structure of the electoral body in Bosnia and Herzegovina. At that time, there was 44.6 per cent of the Muslims in the entire population; however, since that percentage was constituted by a lot of children, there was only 39 per cent of those eligible to vote among them. Now, the situation with Croats was different. There was 17.3 per cent of Croats in the population; however, there was 21 per cent of the Croats eligible to vote. A similar situation existed with the Serbs. The results of the referendum of -- were very clear. Some 40-odd per cent -- or rather 60-odd per cent voted in favour of the independence. Had there been no Serb votes, the referendum would not have been successful. It is therefore certain that the Serbs living in towns in urban areas voted in favour of the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina and it is equally true that the numbers of those that would have voted in favour of the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina would have been much higher had Karadzic and his lot not thwarted the vote in many municipalities where they were in power. I mean in the municipal authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, would you allow me to just ask some clarifying questions on the last answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, you are talking about percentages. You mentioned 44.6 for the Muslims. You also mentioned 17.3 for the Croats. Are these numbers for the whole of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those are official figures from the census of 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The 60 per cent that voted in favour of an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina, was that 60 per cent of calculated on the basis of the whole of the population of Bosnia and Herzegovina or only of those who had voted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 64 per cent actually of the entire population of Bosnia and Herzegovina voted for; whereas .2 or .3 per cent of those who voted were against the independence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now 64 per cent actually of the entire population. So it's not 64 per cent of those who had voted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely correct. No, not of those who voted, 64 per cent of the entire population of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is known that many Serbs did not vote. As far as we have heard until now, the referendum was to a high degree boycotted or Serbs did not participate in the referendum. Do you know how many people -- what was the percentage of the overall population of Bosnia and Herzegovina that participated in the referendum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have told you, 64 per cent. 64 per cent of the citizens participated in the referendum, and out of these, only .2 per cent voted against. .2 per cent of those who turned out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just have a look again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I ask a question about something that is confusing me terribly in the witness's evidence so I don't wish, with respect, to interrupt the flow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you allow me one more question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You told us that some 39 per cent of the population had -- were Muslims which were entitled to vote if we just limit ourselves to the electorate and for the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's precisely my point of confusion. I wonder if I might just ask Your Honour's indulgence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems that you've got similar problems as I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, you said there were 17 -- this is at line 14 on page 12. You said, "There were 17.3 per cent of Croats in the population; however, there was 21 per cent of the Croats eligible to vote." And since 21 is higher than 17.3, that suggests that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just try to check that. Do I understand that the division of the parts of the population, the ethnic groups of the population on the population as a whole was not the same as the division of the ethnic groups if you would just focus on the electorate, that is those who were entitled to vote? That means that on the whole of the population, the percentage of Muslims was higher than the percentage of Muslims that were entitled to vote. That is to say the percentage of Muslims in the electorate. Does that clarify the issue, Mr. Stewart. Because that means that although you may have only 17.3 per cent on the whole of the population, you might have 21 per cent if you just focus on the electorate.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it was the clarification of that answer which is the way it's expressed doesn't -- does potentially confuse.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, may I ask you something just to make sure that I have understood the position correctly. 20 per cent of the electorate were Croats; is that right? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 20, 21 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. And when you were talking about 39 per cent of Muslims, you were saying that 39 per cent of the electorate were Muslims, that's also what you were saying; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And it follows, therefore, that apart from a possibly relatively insignificant category of others, that the other 40 per cent of the electorate were very predominantly Serbs?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, please. You have to understand one thing. The number of citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina was 4.400.000 whereas the number of those who were eligible to vote was 3.4 million. So the ethnic group which had a lot of children was not represented in the electorate in the same percentage as it was represented in the overall population structure. Their percentage of the electorate was smaller. What I'm giving you are official, exact figures that you can obtain from the Institute for Statistics. On the other hand, it has not been established -- just give me a moment to finish my answer ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, yes, but my question is -- you've brought in the population as a whole. My question was very specifically confined to the electorate. So that's what I was asking you. You have been saying that 39 per cent of the electorate were Muslims. You confirmed that specifically. That 20, 21 per cent of the electorate were Croats. You confirmed that specifically. Let's take 21 because it works out neatly arithmetically, if it was 21 per cent Croats and 39 per cent Muslims, that conveniently makes 60 per cent and what I was putting to you therefore was that apart from a possibly insignificant category of others, that the remaining 40 per cent of the electorate were Serbs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No way, no way. Please. I am trying to assist you. I am trying to assist you but I cannot do that unless you are willing to hear what I have to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have a few questions for you, Mr. Kljuic. Try to follow me. We have an electorate, 100 per cent of the electorate. 100 per cent means the total number of those who are entitled to vote; yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You told us that Muslims would be 39 per cent of that electorate; you agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You also told us that 21 per cent of that electorate were Croats; you agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I ask you to follow my assumption I ask you to follow my assumption. My assumption is, just for arguments's sake, all Muslims vote for independence, let's just assume that, yes? Do you agree? Well, you don't.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't have to agree, but I just want you to follow this assumption. Let's just take that. My next assumption is that all Croats also vote in favour of independence. I just ask you to follow that assumption. Yes? On the basis of that assumption, we would have 60 per cent of the electorate of the voters who would vote in favour of independence, that is 39 plus 21. You agree that that would be, on the basis of that assumption, a valid conclusion. Do you still follow me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, Your Honours. It is just the right that belonged to Croats and Muslims, but I would like to ask you: Do you know how many voters actually exercised their right to vote, to turn out at the elections? At the first 1990 elections -- for instance in America, they elected their presidents with only 38 per cent of the electorate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... referendum. In other words, do you know what percentage casted their votes? You said --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We know that: 64 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: All right. Do you know, since there is some information that Serbs had boycotted, do you know exactly which part of the 64 per cent were Muslims, which part were Croats, which part were Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nobody knows that exactly. But what is known is that most of the Croats did turn out. With Muslims, the number of those who cast their votes was important but not everybody did. There were even deputies to the parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina who were against independence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do we know -- you said, "We do know that most of the Croats did turn out." On the basis of what do we know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Based on the organisational work that I did as the president. We have lots of people who are working in Germany and we organise special buses to bring them back to the country to vote. And we know the percentages, municipality by municipality, exact figures of those who turned out to vote. For instance, Grude, where Mate Boban lived, 99 per cent turned out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I might have a language problem but "turn out," could anyone explain to me at this moment what this exactly means in this context?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would understand it to mean went to vote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Went to vote. Do I understand that if you say "turn out" that they went to vote, the Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, are you saying that most of the Croats and most of the Muslims voted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you have no exact figures, what, on the basis of what you learned, would be the percentage? Above 90 per cent Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For Croats, it is certainly over 90 per cent. I'm not sure about the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did the Croats, as far as you know, vote in favour of independence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did the Muslims vote in favour of independence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Most of those who turned out, who cast their votes, voted for independence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what you said 63.8 and 0.2, so that -- well, we restart.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where we might.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: With that electorate of 100, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have 39 out of those 100 being Muslims; do you agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have 21 being Croats.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's now make an assumption that at least 90 per cent, you said for the Croats, it was higher, for the Muslims, you do not know for sure. If I would make the assumption that 90 per cent of Muslims and Croats entitled to vote did vote, would that be a fair assumption? Certainly not less.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure about the Muslims. I'm not sure that over 90 per cent of them voted, but you could assume that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any data on what percentage of the Muslims who were entitled to vote actually did vote?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't. There was a large percentage of Muslims, 39 per cent of those who had the right to vote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's continue on the basis of the 90 per cent assumption. We then have 60 Muslim Croat voters of which 90 per cent comes and votes which means that 54 of them came to vote.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you said 64 per cent voted in favour of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. independence; yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That means that you need 10 more voters from other groups - Serbs, Yugoslavs, whatever - to vote in favour of independence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They wanted to vote. Nobody had to vote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not talking on whether they had to vote. You'd need another 10 out of 100 voters to come to that result. They would be Serbs and others. What percentage of the electorate was Serb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A figure very similar to the Croats, 31 per cent of the population and 32 per cent of the electorate because they had less children, fewer children, just like the Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That means that those remaining would have to add 10 votes out of 100 to get to that result. Mr. Stewart, I'm just asking you whether you follow my analysis at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honour, it's very clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And whether you agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I agree with the arithmetic, Your Honour, based on the assumptions and I understand entirely the assumptions, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the weak spot is that we are working on the basis of assumptions rather than on the basis of established facts. So unless we would have details about that, on this assumption, it would, with the uncertainty what would be the others and what would be the Serbs because that's not clear. But if you would also assume that those 10 votes came in majority from Serbs -- I'm not saying it is so; it could well be others that they were over-represented under these 10 voters. But if not, then approximately one-third of the Serb electorate would have been in favour of the independence, at least voted in favour of independence. So we have a few weak spots, one of them being that we do not know exactly what percentage came to vote, which is a vital piece of information. Because if, overall, it would have been not 90 per cent but 98 per cent, then of course the votes needed by non-Croats, non-Muslims would be considerably less, that would be 2 out of 100, which makes approximately 10 per cent of the Serb or others electorate. I mean it's relatively simple to make the calculations and it's also important to establish how vital the information is on how many Muslims came to vote, how many Croats came to vote because we would then know what you would still need in favour of independence votes to come to the result of 64 per cent. If this is commonly accepted, then the remaining issue is whether we have these data available, yes or no, whether this witness could provide them, or they could be provided by any other source so that we can verify the validity of what the witness told us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would -- thank you very much for that, Your Honour, and as I say, we -- we, I'm royal we or something this morning -- understand Your Honour's analysis based on those assumptions. We do sometimes say in English if we had some fish we could have some fish and chips if we had some chips. So you do really have to explore the assumptions. But Your Honour, I wouldn't propose to explore it further with this witness. This information must be available more conveniently and readily and accurately, with respect, from somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But at least the issue is clear now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's helpful, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour -- as sometimes happen when we have a late start, was Your Honour proposing to just take the first break at the normal time and then proceed according to the normal timetable?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think as a matter of fact we have it a bit later so to split up a in more equal parts but if you prefer to have a break now ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if it's not terribly inconvenient to the Trial Chamber and everybody else because I have made arrangements with various members of my team to meet them and give instructions and so on. So it would be a great help to me Your Honour and since we have just finished this chapter -- I can go on of course for a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll then adjourn until five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm very much obliged for that, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two practical matters. The Chamber will invite the witness to send any notes on meetings he still would have in Sarajevo. I add to that immediately that this should not give rise to any expectations as to the importance, relevance, et cetera. Further written submissions of course can be filed at a later stage and we'll then see what the material is, how important it is, and see what to do with that. But at this moment, the Chamber will invite the witness to provide that material so that the Defence at least has an opportunity to inspect that material. Second question, very practical one, we have an opportunity to move on Friday the 22nd of April from the afternoon session to the morning session which is often considered as a precious thing, the last day of the week moving from the afternoon to the morning. The Judges have no problems. I'd like to hear from the parties if there is any problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We would have no problem, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Neither do we, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then unless there would be problems in terms of interpreter teams, et cetera, et cetera, the Chamber will ask the registry to see whether we could move from the afternoon to the morning session on the 22nd of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I say partly my non-objection was because I didn't even know we were in the afternoon in the first place anyway. Can I take it that -- are we -- if Your Honour can just very helpfully tell me or somebody, are we in the afternoon then for the other days next week?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That week we are scheduled Monday the 18th of April in the morning; Tuesday 19th, Wednesday 20, and Thursday 21 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, that's very helpful. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Usher, could you please escort Mr. Kljuic into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, at page 6.106 of the transcript on the 27th of September last year, you said, and it's -- you've got a number of references to this word. You were asked by Mr. Harmon: "Q. Mr. Kljuic, did you have an opportunity to observe Mr. Krajisnik in his relations with people who were not -- who were Serbs but were not SDS members. Can you describe his views and attitude towards those people." "A. He, just as Karadzic, condemned those people as traitors of Serbdom." Mr. Kljuic, the view of Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik was this, wasn't it, that the SDA and the HDZ were intent upon destruction of Yugoslavia in a way which Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik and all their colleagues regarded as detrimental to the interests of Serbs in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Disagree that that was the view?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, I was in the wrong place.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You disagree that that was the view of, for example, Dr. Karadzic? I just want to know if you disagree about the view or you disagree about the fact, Mr. Kljuic.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree with the notion of non-Serbs having been intent upon destroying Yugoslavia. Yugoslavia was destroyed by Serbs themselves by having pursued non-democratic methods and failed to respect the 1974 Constitution. Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik advocated that very same Serb policy which provoked the reactions of non-Serb ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Just pause for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm quite content not to pursue the resolution of this distinction but I ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's even totally useless.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't put any question to the witness in this respect, so if you would move on to your next subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would find no opposition from the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm very much obliged, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I just put it this way, the word "traitors," Mr. Kljuic, it's a strong, but commonly used word in the rough-and-tumble of politics by party members, representatives, about people who take different view on important issues, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But in the history of the Serbian politics, when they lost the battle at Kosovo Polje, then Brankovic used the term. This term has been widely used in the Balkans, especially with the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, this is a similar matter. If someone uses the word "traitor" of course it's very much depended on the context how defective -- I mean the Chamber is in a position to at least give some meaning and see the relativity which doesn't mean that it doesn't say anything at all, but to see the relativity of the use of the word "traitor."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I wasn't proposing to pursue this point beyond that simple question to the witness anyway. But thank you for that helpful remark, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, the next page of the same transcript, page 6.107, you refer to a Mr. Simovic. You said -- it starts at line 3, "For instance, after the walkout of the SDS in the beginning of the aggression," and you're talking about the walkout October 1991, aren't you there?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One can see here the context of the word "aggression" in -- the aggression on Croatia started in 1991 and on Bosnia in 1992 so that if we are talking about Bosnia here, this isn't the proper context, the proper date.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, it's your evidence. If you don't know -- if you can't work out without a wider context, then say so, but it was the walkout. I was just asking you to confirm that if you can't, you can't, that the walkout that you're referring to was the walkout from the Bosnia-Herzegovina Assembly in October 1991; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you give me the entire sentence please?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm just going to move on, Mr. Kljuic, and withdraw that particular question. Mr. Simovic, you say, "He stayed in Sarajevo after the war started." He was, is this right, he was a member of the Constitutional Court, and he is now a Republika Srpska member, as it were, of the Bosnia and Herzegovina Constitutional Court. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time of the start of the aggression on Bosnia-Herzegovina when he remained in Sarajevo, he was Deputy Prime Minister of the republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Some three to four months after the start of the aggression, he also left Sarajevo. At a later stage, he held certain positions in the Republika Srpska, whether he was a member of the Constitutional Court or a professor on the faculty. And today he's a member of the Constitutional Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did he subsequently leave Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I've said, he was there in the beginning of the aggression as Deputy Prime Minister but after a while, perhaps some three, four, five months later, he left.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you know why he left?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you know of or did you know at the time an academic called Mr. Ekmecic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did he say in Sarajevo and was he arrested by Muslim Croat forces?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was. He remained in Sarajevo for a while. He was arrested. I don't know about that but I do know that he was being bothered, that the government tried to protect him and that he later on went to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you know that he was maltreated in prison?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know but I can assume that he was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The same applied to Mr. Slavko Leovac?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean Leovac. I knew Professor Leovac as well. I believe he shared the same fate of Ekmecic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the same applied to Mr. Svetozar Koljevic and -- if it is Mr. Borisa Starovic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think the same applies to the two of them. Svetozar Koljevic, I knew him very well and I even met him in the street during the war once, whereas Borisa Starovic was my school meat from high school.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you know Professor Najdanovic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I did not know Dr. Najdanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you know of him?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I heard that he had been killed, kidnapped or he otherwise that he went missing and his fate is still unknown today.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But all of the people I've mentioned were prominent Serbs in Sarajevo at the time the conflict began, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We can agree that most of them were distinguished.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And a high proportion of prominent Serbs in Sarajevo were arrested, imprisoned and maltreated when the conflict broke out, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That chaos reigned in the town, that much is true. Some of those were pronounced enemies of the idea of Bosnia-Herzegovina and I here refer to Professor Ekmecic and Borisa Leovac, and there were some groups that went out of hand and wreaked havoc without having been directed to do so by the government. But most importantly, all the citizens in Sarajevo were threatened, endangered at the time, because they had no electricity, food, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, I want to turn to the intercept, please, which was under consideration at page 6.149 of the transcript on the 27th of September last year, and it was tab 31472. It's now an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's Prosecution Exhibit 292, KID number 31472. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the witness is going to be asked questions about the particular intercept, could he be provided of a copy of the intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It depends what questions will be put to him. If he has to have a closer look at it, I expect Mr. Stewart to present it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, yes, indeed, I tend whenever it's fair to the witness and would ultimately be guided by the Trial Chamber on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, this -- I don't know how well you recall this, this is a transcript of a telephone conversation between Mr. Momcilo Mandic and Mr. Krajisnik that took place on the 26th of June, 1992, according to this record. Just to refresh your memory, at page 6.158 of the transcript on Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the 27th of September, Mr. Harmon asked you when the intercepts had been played, Mr. Kljuic, this is page 6.158, "Mr. Kljuic, I played this intercept for you in the context of your previous testimony that dealt with the attitudes of Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik and other attitudes towards non-Serbs who did not subscribe to the SDS agenda. Can I have your comments on observations in respect of this intercept." Your answer was: "A. We see in this conversation the drastic qualifications they give to people who are not towing the line. Although there is an error in the identification of Filip Vukovic. It's true he is a communist but he's not a Serb. He happened to be a Croat. "We see from this that they were sending women and children to us which is another result of ethnic cleansing. But if you wish, we can also see from this that Mr. Krajisnik was involved in many problems beginning with exchanges with the Muslims because this person, Karamehmedovic had been sent to Sarajevo, and in exchange some people were demanded from Sarajevo." Mr. Kljuic, do you know who Mr. Karamehmedovic was?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So if I suggest to you that he was a former colleague of Mr. Krajisnik's who had been arrested by the VRS, you know nothing that would contradict that suggestion?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So if you were told that this was a personal appeal to Mr. Krajisnik to become involved in obtaining the release of one of his former colleagues, again, you know nothing to contradict that assertion.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't except perhaps for the fact that he would use his offices for a friend to be released but not for someone who was not a friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I wonder, Your Honour, perhaps the witness should see the copy of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you see the first reference that you can find in this document to Mr. Karamehmedovic? Do you see that? The first time his name is mentioned, can you find that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, in the transcript it's at page 6.151 at line 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Then about ten lines on from that, there's a reference to 400 prisoners. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see where Karamehmedovic is mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I thought you had that, then. If you go on about 10 or 12 lines it should be, you see a reference -- do you see: "Mandic Momcilo: I've got 400." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then Mr. Krajisnik says, "And who is criticising?" Mr. Mandic says, "This Filip Vukovic, this member of the youth organisation, Serb, he says clean it, but for them they are..." And then it goes on a few lines. Mr. Krajisnik says, "What does he want?"

utterances.speaker: MR. MANDIC
utterances.text: "He is president of the exchange commission. Their commission. "Yes. "And what is it that he wants? "War prisoners. No, they are ex for them. They are hardly interested in people. They are interested in ammunition and meat and now we let those women and children to go to Vrbanja... to go to their own people. He said that's ethnic cleansing what we're doing..." Mr. Kljuic, my first question is whether you know any more about this particular matter about women and children going to Vrbanja than what we can read here in this transcript.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of all of the parts of the town of Sarajevo, Grbavica was in the most difficult situation because it was cut off from the rest of the town as bridges were connecting it to them. It was a neighbourhood that was very close to the surrounding mountains and was placed under Serb control very early on with the help of the JNA. There were examples of families divided between Grbavica and Sarajevo and many tried to cross over to town proper as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was whether you had any specific knowledge of this event, that is women and children sent to Vrbanja. You are a he not asked about what the context of this might have been but whether you have any specific knowledge of this event.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Vrbanja is a bridge that separated the warring parties. It was at this bridge that exchanges were conducted. I don't know the details but I know that many people from Sarajevo went over to the Serb-controlled territory across Vrbanja and from Serb-controlled territory crossed over to the town proper; and that in addition to the arrangements made by individual persons, there were also commissions that engaged in the exchange of prisoners and most often of common citizens. Therefore, they were not exchanging troops but citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, can we take it that whatever you just said, you don't know anything about this particular matter that is referred to here the women and children going to Vrbanja?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about these women, about Karamehmedovic. I don't know anything specific about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, on the basis of the text of the telephone intercept, one could even wonder whether this was one specific event or that it was a development. "Now we let these women and children" could also be a specific group or it could also be a practice that was developed or had developed. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I note and understand Your Honour's comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You said in your evidence and I don't have the specific reference to this, Mr. Kljuic, but I doubt that you will dispute it, that Croats were not supporting Bosnia remaining part of Yugoslavia because that would mean remaining part of Greater Serbia. That's -- that accurately represents your view, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What was the concern of Croats in remaining part of Greater Serbia?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they had a second-rate position in the former Yugoslavia, both in the Yugoslavia ruled by the Karadjordjevic dynasty and in the Yugoslav version. In the Greater Serbia, they would have the position of Croats in today's Vojvodina who are not even entitled to newspapers or radio in their own language.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the concern of the Bosnian Serbs was to be in a minority in Bosnia and Herzegovina, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, that is not true. Nobody would have been a minority. On the contrary, they would be equal. We Croats could arguably be a minority. I personally authored a document which could have secured the constitutional rights of all ethnic communities. And you have among the documentation I supplied my letter to President Tudjman --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, let me stop you for one second. Mr. Stewart, we heard so much evidence on the issue of who would be a minority in what circumstances and, of course, what a minority is differs from the point of view one is taking, whether that would be minority in respect of a absolute majority of others or whether that would be a minority in respect of a coalition of others, none of them having an absolute majority. To have this explained again by the witness that the Bosnian Serbs would not be a minority, I could spell out whatever could be said about that without even having to look at my papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't wish it to be explained, Your Honour. That was not what I was looking for. Some of these points are single-question points. If the witness simply answers my question, I will move on as I would be very happy to do on that particular point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, I want to hand you, please, one of the items that you have supplied previously to the Trial Chamber, not the ones that arrived yesterday. It's item 14 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's D40. And Madam Registrar is still waiting to receive a copy of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We can supply a copy, Your Honour, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's the one we looked at yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I just want to ask you, towards the end of this account that you give of the meeting in question in September 1991, you said that, "two days" -- it's about four paragraphs from the end. "Two days after these failed negotiations, I went to see Tudjman in Zagreb. When we exchanged information about the situation, I told him about the talks with SDS leaders. He was very glad to hear that I'd held a meeting on the level of HDZ and SDS leadership. When I told him about the outcome of the talks, he became lost in thought" and so on. Mr. Kljuic, did you make notes either during the meeting with Mr. Tudjman or -- notes of this meeting either during the meeting or at some point afterwards?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never took notes from my own discussions with President Tudjman. But a huge number of those discussions was audiotaped and were published two months ago in two volumes published by the Split newspaper Feral. A detailed record was given on all the views of President Tudjman on Bosnia and his discussions with the representatives of Croats and others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kljuic, just to make it clear, during that meeting with Mr. Tudjman, you made no notes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We see that you've written down in this document. Was that the first time that you did write down what was said during that meeting or were there any previous writings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. This is the only thing I have. The whole meeting was initiated pursuant to the order of Mr. Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's a clear answer. You have no further notes. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And when you said a moment ago - excuse me - "That a huge number of these discussions was audiotaped," these discussions, are you including or meaning your own meeting just referred to with Mr. Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I received these books very recently and I'm having a hard time reading them. I haven't yet established whether that particular detail is on record in that book, but some meetings that took place previously are included and I believe the transcripts are given in chronological order.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm just trying to get clear, Mr. Kljuic, what you're talking about. Because you refer to "these discussions" in very wide terms as having been audiotaped and published by Feral Tribune, I think it's called, isn't it. What discussions, what range of discussions, what type of discussions is covered by these audiotape transcripts, presumably published by Feral Tribune?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a huge volume including several hundred discussions that took place on a variety of occasions. Most of them have to do with Bosnian Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, one topic; Bosnian Croats and Yugoslavia being another topic. And I, as Croat number one had discussions, Boban, Tudjman, Susak and other conversations. I found another conversations where I clashed with Zagreb concerning their policy towards Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So your conversation or conversations with Mr. Tudjman were included in these published discussions, were they?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Most of them seemed to be included. I don't know for sure, it's a huge volume, I have to study it yet. But it is a very important material from which you can see the positions taken by certain individuals at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What's it called? It's a book, is it, published by Feral Tribune?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It's called "The Transcripts." About the division of Bosnia. Your own person in Sarajevo can obtain it in Sarajevo and sent it to you. It's very simple. It consists of two volumes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sure I can when I find out who he or she is, Mr. Kljuic. I would like you to have item 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I have a clean copy myself, Your Honour. Item 15 of the first batch of items that was supplied by Mr. Kljuic to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that you'd like to have number 15 assigned a D number as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I would indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would be D41, I take it, Madam Registrar. Yes, it's confirmed by Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, this is -- apart from the number in the corner and 15 but that doesn't perhaps matter. This is a typed document and this is something that you have written; is that right, Mr. Kljuic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And can you say when you wrote it?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote it partly at the time when it was happening and later, I compiled it all in a single piece of writing that was finalised in the form in which it will be published in a book.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, it relates largely to what is called the historic agreement, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you've just, in a nutshell, given your summary of what the historic agreement was.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see the changes of the constitutional order of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the transition from a totalitarian to a democratic system were supposed to take place on two levels. One had to do with the issue of how to organise the Yugoslav community, and the second had to deal with the structuring of Bosnia and Herzegovina. All of this was supposed to be done within the institutions of the system. However, it didn't work out that way due to the extreme demands of Slobodan Milosevic and the non-observance of the 1974 Constitution including the principle of equality among nations. But let us set aside the problems on the level of Yugoslavia. Let us just look at the problem in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Instead of insisting the discussions take place in the parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina with harmonisation of views on what the future should be, a trick was used so that Muslims, nowadays Bosniaks, be excluded from the institutions of the system and that a separate agreement be made between Croats and Serbs -- between Serbs and Muslims putting Croats before a fait accompli. I witnessed this because Mr. Koljevic's office was next to mine in the building of the Presidency. And I warned them that this bilateral agreement between Serbs and Muslims would mean an end to Bosnia and Herzegovina as we knew it. I even waited for them on one occasion when they were coming out of an office and I told them, "Gentlemen, when you agree, you have to come to see me." The principal political force of Bosnian Muslims was the SDA party. It was not involved. Instead, a small, a very small Bosnian Muslim party was involved in this. Their leaders, their representatives went to Belgrade and tried to elicit the support of Muslims by saying that if the two largest nations in Bosnia come to an agreement, the war Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. could be avoided. However, this agreement was never reached. It fell through, and this failure can be blamed on a lot of people. Because if that agreement had become reality, then Yugoslavia would have fallen apart in quite a different way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You say in this document, it's the end of the first paragraph, -- well, it's about five lines from the end. You say, "Alija Izetbegovic and I never became close friends partly because we are completely different from each other and perhaps even more importantly, because at that time, he already had plans that were different from mine." "At that time," what date would you put on "at that time"?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was year 1991. You see, the problem of Bosnia and Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What part of 1991?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second half, autumn 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you say, "Izetbegovic" -- "I had no choice, however. Izetbegovic supported BH, Bosnia Herzegovina, or at least said so and Karadzic openly threatened the sovereignty of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Now, first of all, "Mr. Izetbegovic supported Bosnia and Herzegovina." Do you mean by that supported sovereignty of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but the problem of Bosnia and Herzegovina was entirely different. I personally would have asked for a civic state. But in Bosnia and Herzegovina, you cannot underestimate the national aspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, then Mr. Izetbegovic, according to you, "or at least said so." So you at the time, did you, had, at the very least, very severe reservations about whether Mr. Izetbegovic meant what he was saying?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not have reservations. I even had no prospects. Karadzic was openly against an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina and Izetbegovic wanted it. However in this correlation and the religious, the position wasn't clear. To date, we have not found a solution for Bosnia in which it would be a civic state with adequate protection for religious freedoms. It is very difficult in Bosnia because of the internal relationships, traditions, and the complicated nature of life. However, Izetbegovic was indeed in favour of Bosnia and that was crucial.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You talk, and in the English, it's in the middle of the second page, just to pick up a reference, do you see a reference in -- it's your document. Do you see a reference in this document, perhaps about a third of the way through to "600.000 Muslims from Turkey ..."? Do you see that reference 600.000?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Well following on from that, that's just a reference point. The next paragraph we get that paragraph that I think may be from somewhere else we considered yesterday about your superiority and Mr. Karadzic from the Dermitor mountains and then you record, "He won't do anything if you and your Serbs support Bosnia and Herzegovina, I said." Now, that is you talking to Dr. Karadzic, is it?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then the next bit, "How come you and I disagree when our bosses have the same position on Bosnia and Herzegovina?" Is that -- according to you, is that Dr. Karadzic talking, is it, or you?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, that's so self-evident in the context of this conversation that I really -- if the answer in the context of a conversation is "Remember Radovan, I have no political boss," then of course the previous one could be words spoken by Karadzic. It's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I accept that. When I was reading through a moment ago, I had actually felt it was not sufficiently self-evident but I now see that it was. My apologies, Your Honour. I now see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And he was -- those are his exact words, are they, as far as you recall?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean Dr. Karadzic's words?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And first noted by you how long after the conversation?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot tell you that. You know why? Because when this whole story about historic agreements started, then I wrote this sentence by sentence, excerpt by excerpt, then they went to Belgrade to sign something and didn't sign it and then it was all wrapped up. But if you really want to know, I can tell you that this is Karadzic's statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, the question was: How long after the conversation you noted it down. You said, "Well, I cannot tell you that." That's an answer to the question. The next question might have been whether you would have a time frame but that's just what Mr. Stewart asked you. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Then you go back to, in this record, whatever it is, you go back to the conversation you had with Izetbegovic and you say, "An offer had allegedly been made to him for the Muslims to remain in Yugoslavia and he would then become the president of the Assembly in Yugoslavia." Then it is you saying, "It's true, you could be the president of the Assembly; however, it would not be the Assembly of Yugoslavia but that of Serbia." "So you're saying that they made you an offer for your people to be --" and there's a question mark in English, it's the "second largest in Yugoslavia." Is that what your note says in the original?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That was the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And it goes on: "And who is the second largest people in Serbia today? The ethnic Albanians. There, they're offering you the same position as the ethnic Albanians now have, I said." Now, where you said "It would not be the Assembly of Yugoslavia but that of Serbia," what precisely were you meaning there?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is clear that thereby, Muslims would have remained in a rump Yugoslavia in which Serbs would have an absolute majority and Muslims would indeed be the people number two in that state, that they would not have the parliamentary power to have any decision they wanted actually voted for.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then you say that Mr. Izetbegovic "... ended the conversation by saying quietly, as if to himself, 'No it's not going to happen.'" Was that said so that -- in a way that Mr. Izetbegovic would have known that you heard what he said?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, and he sort of waved his hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stewart. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have no additional questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I might have a few. I'm afraid that I'm badly organised because I ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I apologise for being badly organised because the underlying material I would like to confront the witness with is not in my binder here at this moment. I suggest that we take a break now, that I have one or two or three questions for you, Mr. Kljuic, and that might be the end of your examination. In order not to waste any further time, I'd like to have a break now for 20 minutes so we'll continue at 25 minutes past 12.00 and the parties should then prepare for the next witness to be called after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, I've got a few questions for you. They are related to some intercepts we heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The first and very simple question: Do you know who Mr. Milinkovic.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Short question, short answer. Thank you for that. Then we heard an intercept, a conversation between Jovan Tintor and Mr. Krajisnik of the 4th of April 1992. I'm going to read a small portion of that conversation to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TINTOR SAYS
utterances.text: "Look, I called you this morning to... to check about this thing, these people from Slavonski Brod have been calling me... fuck, military." Mr. Krajisnik then says, "Look, Simovic and Joko have gone there. I called down there. The SDS and HDZ representatives, they will receive them. Go there and try to calm the situation down. I know that this vice-president of theirs from the HDZ, what was his name?"

utterances.speaker: MR. TINTOR SAYS
utterances.text: "Um-um --"

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK SAYS
utterances.text: "He will, because there seems to be a third party that's trying to mess this up and it doesn't suit neither Muslim, neither Croats, nor Serbs that there is chaos there." This is a conversation about events that happened in Slavonski Brod close to the 4th of April, 1992. Do you have any personal knowledge of what happened exactly in Slavonski Brod?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
