utterances.text: I have to tell you that the town of Slavonski Brod is in the Republic of Croatia. Perhaps this has to do with Bosanski Brod which is in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you then know anything that happened in Bosanski Brod at that very moment?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation in Bosanski Brod was very difficult because a large number of civilians was fleeing to Croatia where, at that time, peace already prevailed. Whether the Yugoslav Peoples' Army wanted to control the bridge or not, I cannot tell you. But during the war in Croatia, this bridge was, in part, made unpassable. This is the route that is most frequently used between Slovenia and Croatia on the one hand, and the southern part of what was formerly Yugoslavia. I don't know the details, but if this has to do with Posavina and the vice-president of HDZ, that was Niko Stanic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Was that bridge impassable already on the 4th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tanks and trucks and cars could not cross over it, but I believe that pedestrians could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Then finally, I'd like to take you back to your testimony of the 29th of September, page 6.306. You were asked about a telephone conversation between Mr. Stojic and Mr. -- no, no, I'm making a mistake. At that time, it was Mr. Kvesic and Mr. Mandic speaking to each other. I'll just read a small part of that.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if I may, Mr. Kvesic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Branko Kvesic.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Branko Kvesic, Momo Mandic, Bruno Stojic and I don't know what Stanisic's first name is. But that was the conversation, the four of them. Mico Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well I read just one part of a conversation between Kvesic and Mandic on the 5th of May, 1992. Mr. Kvesic said, "So you are right there in Pale, are you?" Mandic: "Well, we are not. We came down to the city." Kvesic: "Yes. Yes." Mandic: "We came down and cleaned Grbavica..." Kvesic: "Is that so?" Mandic: There we hold Ilidza, Dobrinja, and Nedzarici, all the way to student campus and so on." You were asked questions about this telephone conversation on the 29th of September, and part of your answer, page 6.306 was after you -- you said the following: "And already then Mandic is reporting and saying that Grbavica is being cleared and the greater crime was committed at Grbavica which was otherwise a multi-ethnic settlement." Then you summarized that. You said something about taking over the police school in Vrace, and then you continue: "It's densely populated area and when he says -- when Momo Mandic says that they have cleaned Grbavica, that means that they have -- that they took away many people. Some they killed. Some went in for exchange so that Grbavica already at that period of time, when this conversation took place in May, actually it had already been in ethnically cleaned, cleansed. And he is bragging to Kvesic about this." That was your answer.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge of cleaning or cleansing of Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I do. I visited a lady immediately after the liberation of Grbavica. The lady was a proofreader in the editing house, newspaper house of Oslobodjenje where I first started working as a journalist. Her name is Maja Fulanovic. At that point, I saw a woman who had spent four years in a room, one of the few Catholics to have survived in Grbavica thanks to the assistance of her neighbour Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you. First of all, if you say "After the liberation of Grbavica," you may be aware that what is a liberation and what is an aggression is looked at from different points of view. Do I understand by the liberation that you mean when Grbavica was not under Serb control anymore?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm speaking from my point of view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you give that a date?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was immediately after the reintegration which began in early 1996. I can't tell you the exact date. But I know for a fact about this and I have a witness who went with me. He was a well-known --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So your answer is that was the date is early 1996. Now, you started telling us -- what I'd like to know is whether you have any personal knowledge, not reconstruction after a couple of years, but what did you see or hear at the time you said Grbavica was cleaned or cleansed.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I do not have firsthand knowledge because I wasn't there. But many people who had fled over from there came to see me. Like for instance the academician Ciglar, a first-rate intellectual, also a Croat, who had survived those very difficult circumstances and once Grbavica was liberated, he came over to see me and thank me. There are many other people who were either exchanged or managed to flee from there, told me about what the situation was like in Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell me what exactly they told you, those who were exchanged, one of the categories.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I was interested in knowing how some of the people fared in Grbavica, I had many friends there, I was told that the poet Jakov Jurisic had been killed, that many people had been killed. There were also different cases when someone from Belgrade or Serbia went over there and fetched people to save them. I've also heard stories like that. There is a lot of written material as well produced by eyewitnesses who wanted to portray the situation as it was in Grbavica at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Those exchanged, were they kept in detention before they were exchanged? Did they tell you about that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them were kept in detention, others weren't. Others were in hiding in different homes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were they civilians?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of them were. There were no military formations, either Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. those of the military or of the Territorial Defence in Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then you said that people were killed, that you were told that people were killed. Did they tell you how they were killed?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not, I did not learn any such information; however, as some of the bodies were exhumed from graves one could learn that most of them were killed as a result of an injury by a blunt object or as a result of a gunshot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Which leaves it still open that they were intentionally killed or that they were hit by a bullet although not being specifically targeted.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, far from anything specific. And I cannot claim with any certainty this might have been the case; however, this was a campaign. When Mr. Mandic says that everything was cleansed in one month, then you can imagine what sort of hell it must have been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The only thing I was trying to do to see whether apart from this telephone conversation that you would have specific knowledge on what happened in Grbavica. Apart from this -- these words spoken by the person who took part in that telephone conversation. Thank you very much for your answers. Any further questions? Mr. Stewart, not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Kljuic, perhaps I -- First, Mr. Stewart. At this moment in view of the notes - I hardly dare to use the word - is there anything -- the Chamber has very much in mind at this moment, also in view of what the 37 page the witness has brought us both on paper and in examination that it is -- well, it's not the most relevant material we've seen during this trial. The Chamber would suggest that if the material received now and any material we hopefully receive after I've invited the witness to send it to us would raise any further need to specifically pay attention to it, that written submissions could be filed in that respect. But I leave it to you to address us and to say whether you would think that another approach would be more appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour is talking of written submissions as to, for example, the question of whether Mr. Kljuic should then be cross-examined further?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I didn't use those words, but if you --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's hard to avoid it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it's in your mind, I do understand, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure what other process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I didn't want to encourage you in that sense, but.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I need no encouragement, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It doesn't surprise me that it was on your mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well of course it is, Your Honour, because I've made that very clear because after all, we're talking about the -- we must, with respect, we suggest, Your Honour, all be extremely open-minded about it because we simply do not know what might arrive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Therefore no door is closed and if the Defence think that there is any need to further cross-examine Mr. Kljuic on the basis of any notes either received yet but not yet translated, or any notes still to be received, we'd like to receive written submissions on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour. May I also just inquire briefly, Your Honour, it may be -- there seems to be some breakdown of communication over which I've made a request of the Trial Chamber, but would it be appropriate for the Defence, and of course the Prosecution would have the same opportunity, to ask -- I think it's what happened before, to comment on any draft communication to be sent to Mr. Kljuic in relation to this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if there's any need to further communicate with Mr. Kljuic, I'll address an invitation to Mr. Kljuic now. If there's any need for further communication in writing, then first the other party should be informed about it. If the Chamber would address Mr. Kljuic, you would be informed about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm very much obliged, Your Honour. May I respectfully suggest that it just really wouldn't be a bad idea if whatever Your Honour were about to say were followed up with a written communication to avoid any possible misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take note of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, a lot has been said -- no, no, please remain seated. Mr. Kljuic, a lot has been said about notes, notes made at the time; notes of meetings; notes further included in draft sections of your book. This morning, you specifically said to Mr. Stewart that there still might be some notes you have made of meetings in 1991, 1992. You also said that you are willing to review your material and to see whether there is still any there. You also said that you would be willing to send it to the Tribunal. May I invite you to do that. And would that be possible to do that within, well, let's say the next two weeks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I lose a lot of time coming here and going back and I'm currently advisor for foreign relations -- for foreign policy in the government and I currently have a lot of work there. I have come here for the reasons stated before, although I am recovering from my illness. And you have said that I should give them to you within two weeks. I will do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I just was trying to find out whether two weeks would be a reasonable time. If you say -- if you are more comfortable with three weeks ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I find the material sooner, in three days, I will send it forthwith. You have to understand me that it's a room full of papers, newspapers, articles, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, we have full understanding for your daily schedule especially having recovered from your illness. The Chamber invites you to send within the next three weeks any additional material you would find. We'll send you a short letter to confirm that and then we'll see whether to what that finally will lead, what it leads to anything in this courtroom, yes or no. Mr. Kljuic, you've come already two times now, you've spent five days in this courtroom. I'd like to thank you for answering questions of both parties and the Bench and I wish you not only a safe trip home again, but also a further good recovery from your illness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, I think exhibits in respect to Mr. Kljuic have not been dealt with yet -- the Prosecution have. Then there's only the remainder which is I think D40 and D41. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then they are admitted into evidence. The new procedure is that we just call the numbers and that the parties are in the position to give any comment on the final description of the documents in the list as prepared by the registry. Is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If I may have leave of the Court, Your Honour. Mr. Margetts will be involved with the next witness and he will respond, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, would Your Honours mind if I could stay tor a few minutes and then slip out as quietly as I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any functional absence due to the change of witnesses, permission is granted for the rest of this trial. But I of course appreciate the politeness shown by both parties. Mr. Margetts, no protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: No protective measures, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Just prior to that, Your Honour, there is an issue I need to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could it be raised in the presence of the witness or would we prefer to have that done --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I think it's preferable in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we will ask Mr. Usher to wait for a few moments before the witness is brought in. Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I just indicated to the court that I received a second supplemental information sheet in relation to this witness at approximately 11.30 a.m. by e-mail this morning. Now, Your Honour, there was a prior supplemental information sheet that's dated 7th of April. That's last week. Now, Your Honours, firstly, that sort of lateness is not acceptable. Secondly -- particularly in view of the fact that the witness is being interviewed since the apparently from -- from the face of the supplemental sheet, from the 7th of April. Thirdly, I've spoken to Mr. Margetts prior to Your Honours coming on the bench and he indicated as far as he was concerned, there was no real difference between the supplemental information sheet of one sentence and one paragraph of the 7th of April and the supplemental information sheet extending over a page of the 11th of April. I will allow Your Honours to be the judge of the differences between the supplemental information sheets and I hand them up for this purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We will receive them. But first of all, Mr. Margetts, is there any explanation for the 7th of April where we are living the 12th today or do you disagree.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I disagree with two things. The supplemental information sheet is not an important issue but it was provided as 11.08 not 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's great.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Secondly, the representation that I have suggested there's no difference is not a representation I made. I don't know how it's being perceived that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. What I asked you was about the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry, apologies. Yes, the witness arrived on the Wednesday last week and as Your Honour knows, I've been heavily involved in the witness that preceded Mr. Kljuic, Mr. Trbojevic. And so my meetings with him on the Thursday and the Friday of last week have been short. I did have an opportunity to meet with him yesterday for a longer period. The -- immediately upon receiving some additional information last Thursday, we provided that to the Defence. Immediately upon receiving the additional information or some corrections yesterday, we proceeded to put that in a form of a supplemental information sheet. Obviously the supplemental information sheets can be provided late in the evening on the day that that supplemental information is provided and both the Prosecution and Defence do work late into the evening so that's the usual course. It is clear that this was not what occurred with this supplemental information sheet but it was provided at 11.00. Our position is this: That on this particular supplemental information sheet, the information relates to matters that are either substantially within the Defence's knowledge from the previous statement and amounts to small corrections, or alternatively matters that can be easily perceived and incorporated by Defence in their analysis of the evidence that's to be provided. Supplemental information sheets by their very nature, are an advantage to the Defence. Ordinarily if there was not proofing, the Defence would find out about these corrections and this additional information in the course of examination-in-chief which is not prior to the witness arriving here. So in this instance, I see that practically, the Defence has benefited by the information we've provided and the dispute seems to be as to whether it should have been provided late last night --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: -- or early this morning. And frankly, Your Honour, we do our best to provide it at the earliest possible time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Was it -- was the information sheet prepared yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, it was prepared yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then there's no reason why not that takes just ten seconds to send it by e-mail to Ms. Loukas so that Ms. Loukas is master of her time to the extent possible, which is not a great extent anyhow. So let that be clear. I mean either late in the evening you finish by sending an e-mail or you start in the morning by sending an e-mail. I think it's fair that it should be done late in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just for the record say that it was not the intent of the Prosecution for this to go out this morning but it did go out this morning. But our point is that really, this amounts to absolutely no prejudice to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It doesn't change what I just said. Ms. Loukas, could we be provided with the supplemental information sheet.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. This is the supplemental information sheet of the 7th of April and this is the one that arrived this morning which I indicated was approximately 11.30 but I am so thankful that Mr. Margetts points out it's 11.08 because it so added to his argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, could you tell us what bothers you most, I take it especially in the 11.08.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, indeed, I don't think it's hardly a point and I don't propose to address it. It is of no real consequence and of course I think that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say it's -- we are not going -- it will not -- we'll not cause to ask us for further delays to examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No, I shouldn't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's then proceed, but at the same time, I think you've made your point. The last thing we do before going to sleep is to ask ourselves whether we have sent every material to the other party. That's the basic message.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that's certainly what I do before I go to sleep. And I would recommend to Mr. Margetts he does the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Margetts are you ready to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we're ready to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you please escort Mr. Omeragic into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Omeragic. Can you hear me in a language you understand? Mr. Omeragic, before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that will you speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. The Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. text is now handed out to you by the usher. I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly swear that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated, Mr. Omeragic. You will first be examined by Mr. Margetts, counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Margetts, before you start, is my recollection correct that it is three hours on --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, four hours was what we had specified. I have indicated to the Defence that we may possibly be quicker than that but we would be in a better position to judge that at the end of the first session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Margetts. On the basis of what the Chamber has seen, that is the statement, if you focus at what really -- if at least the testimony is about what he has told you in the statement, it could be done without any problem in half that time. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, you will attempt to expedite the examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Omeragic, could you please state your full name for the Court.

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: My name is Sead Omeragic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And Mr. Omeragic, you were born on the 7th of July 1958 in Trebinje, Bosnia and Herzegovina and your ethnicity is Bosniak; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: In 1982, you graduated from Sarajevo University and in 1983, you commenced your career which you are still pursuing as a journalist; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, as far as the CV is concerned which is the first part of his statement, would there be any problem if we would refer to the statement in that respect?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No problem whatsoever, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: When the war commenced in Bosnia and Herzegovina were you working for the newspaper Slobodna Bosna?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: In early 1992, that's early April 1992, did you learn that forces commanded by Arkan, Zeljko Raznjatovic, had assumed control or Bijeljina city and a delegation of the Presidency of SR BiH had failed to gain access to the town on or around the 2nd of April?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just in relation to that we've actually gone straight into the heart of the question via a leading question and I do object to that. The sort of information that needs to be elicited about the Presidency and what have you should, in my submission, be led from the witness without leading questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, I see in the statement about the visit on the 4th of April and how important and relevant is it that that two days earlier, as you suggested in your question, that a visit failed?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not an important matter, it was really a matter of trying to set the logic up for Your Honours. But if Your Honours have read the statement then we don't need this information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may have taken from my earlier objections that we have. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: On the 4th of April, 1992, a further delegation visited Bijeljina including Fikret Abdic, Biljana Plavsic, General Prascevic and yourself and you accompanied Fikret Abdic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: When you Fikret Abdic, you did so in the guise of his body guard Fikret Abdic having told you that you were too large physically to appear as his chief of cabinet; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Would you tell the Court what Fikret Abdic was and what his position was at the time and who General Prascevic what and what his position was at the time.

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Fikret Abdic was a member of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which was then the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and he was one of six members of the Presidency. General Prascevic was some sort of man number two in the 2nd Corps of the army under the command of General Kukanjac who was based in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to present the first exhibit to the witness. That's the article that was published on the 10th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The exhibit may be presented to the witness. Is that the same as attached to the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it part of the statement? Would it be included in the statement if tendered and admitted into evidence? You understand what I mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it's not exhibited to the statement formally on the first page of the statement but it is referred to and explained in the second paragraph of the statement so we would tender it with the statement, if the statement was to go into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As an attachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So at this need moment, to need to give it a separate exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, would you like us to tender the statement with the attachment at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We could give it an exhibit number at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you want to tender that? It's not entirely clear whether you have any 89 (F) in mind or not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, this is a viva voce because we didn't intend tendering the statement but it's really not a matter that we have a position on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's then take the -- let's then take the article as an exhibit. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Prosecution Exhibit P584.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that's the publication with the headline "The Bloody Bajram in Bijeljina," of the 10th of April, 1992. Please proceed, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Omeragic, the article that you have before you, is that an article you wrote upon your return from Bijeljina and was published in Slobodna Bosna on the 10th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Omeragic. I have no further questions in relation to that exhibit. I'd like now to turn to your travel to Bijeljina. Is it correct that you drove in a convoy of around of about five cars? You were in one car with Fikret Abdic and Biljana Plavsic was in another vehicle in the same convoy.

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was in Mr. Abdic's car and I was seated right behind his official driver. His bodyguard was sitting next to me. Mrs. Biljana Plavsic, in her car, was most of the time behind us. She was in the car together with her driver and her bodyguard. I don't believe they had a fourth passenger. And another vehicle was the jeep of General Prascevic. He had his own escorts including a young man that I knew. I believe he had the rank of staff sergeant. There were some police escorts, but they weren't much help in crossing the checkpoints we encountered on the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Omeragic. When you passed through the city of Ugljevik which I believe is about 15 minutes outside of Bijeljina, could you describe to the Court what you observed there in terms of the presence of military personnel.

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: First we reached a barricade where an old yellow truck was placed across the road like a roadblock and there were large piles of sand in addition to the truck so it was very difficult to pass through. Even later when they allowed us through, I looked to the side and I saw some civilians who had their guns trained on us. We were stopped originally by uniformed persons who I believe belonged to the Territorial Defence, some 7 or 8 of them. We negotiated for a while about whether they would allow us to go through. Mrs. Biljana Plavsic talked to them and it seemed to work; however, all of us representatives from the media were forced to turn around and go back and even later, whenever journalists wanted to come to Bijeljina from Sarajevo, they had to use different roads. I was the only one on that occasion from the Sarajevo media to pass through. Every 200 metres or so we would run into a new checkpoint. One was manned by soldiers dressed in olive-green/grey uniforms. They stood there almost frozen like statues, watching cars pass by.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: What ethnicity were the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: I believe they had to be Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: You said that you were the only member of the Sarajevo media allowed through at that time. Was that because you were presented as the bodyguard of Fikret Abdic?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: I believe that was the only reason, otherwise I would have never passed through.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: As you entered Bijeljina, did you observe anything about the houses?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Well, I looked around. I was very interested in seeing what the whole thing looked like. And one had to notice inevitably that all the shutters were down, all the windows were hidden behind the shutters. It was only once that a woman appeared through the shutters in the window. I was able to see her because we were not going very fast. Her face was about 10 metres away from me and there was fear in her eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: As you entered Bijeljina, did you see a mosque and, if so, what did you observe about that mosque?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: I observed as we were entering Bijeljina that the the Serbian flag was flying on top of the great mosque I believe it is the largest mosque in Bijeljina on the tower. I saw that flag and I remember turning to Mr. Abdic in the car and saying, "Look where they hoisted the flag." It was only when we had gone on another 10 metres that Abdic said suddenly, "What are you talking about? What flag?" As if it took him that long to think about it. However, the driver stopped the car and we got out and the driver said, "Yes, there is indeed a flag hoisted on top of the mosque." And Abdic said, "Never mind, go on." However, we had all seen the flag before we started again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Later on and we'll get to this in your evidence, but you did tour the town and you spoke to various people. In your conversations with these people, did you hear any further information about the mosques in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: I know there was a flag on the second mosque as well which is in the city park and I also know that when Mr. Abdic wanted to enter the mosque in the park, he was not allowed to. And the way he was forbidden from entering is also strange. At one point, a sniper started shooting over our heads and people panicked, but Abdic's driver said that there was a sniper on top of the mosque so this whole attempt fell through. In front of me, there were two Arkan's men and I heard them talking and we were going around the town, they were talking precisely about that and they were saying something like, "It would be a real surprise if they went into the mosque." Another thing was inside the mosques, people were saying victims were being hidden from public view. That may have been the reason why they didn't let Mr. Abdic go in. Another thing I heard was that the mosques were looted on the first day. I heard these men talking about it saying that it was the local Serbs who had done it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: At some stage did you turn on radio in the car and, if so, what did you hear?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: As one point as we were entering Bijeljina, something happened that was perhaps the greatest shock of all to me. Radio Semberija from Majevica, which is in fact the Bijeljina main radio, broadcast that 25 bodies had been found on the main garbage dump in the town. And I couldn't keep quiet in the car, I was so impressed that I said to the others in the car, "Did you hear this, that 25 bodies had been found on the garbage dump?" And Abdic, as if wanting to deny it said, "What are you talking about? What is it that you heard?" However, the bodyguard and the driver, although they must have heard it, did not support me, probably out of respect for Abdic. And we just continued on our way without further comment. But it stuck in my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Again, we will refer to your tour of the town but whilst you were touring the town, did anyone give you similar information about the garbage dump whilst you were on the tour?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: I don't remember whether it was exactly on the garbage dump but I remember that Arkan's men were never far away from us as we were touring the town, one or two metres away from me at all times. At one point I approached the people from the Territorial Defence, the uniformed men and asked one of them, seeking any sort of information, I said, in fact, "It's a good thing that you slaughtered those balijas." And the man said, "Yes, it's good we killed them." There was also some information about some murders I got from a woman who intercepted me in front of the town hall. I talked to her, in fact, I tried to comfort her as far as I could. Her face had an unhealthy colour. She was very disappointed and upset talking about some people who wanted to get out of Bijeljina at any cost. I realised later that she was a Serb woman. But even she, as it turns out, wanted to leave Bijeljina. I believe she was a member of some liberal party. She talked about some murders and some horrors. I had another encounter after we visited the hospital. I believe I'll have to come back to that later. I had another encounter --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Omeragic. I'll ask you specific questions about each of those encounters as we approach them in a chronological sequence; however, since you have mentioned this woman, can you confirm that this woman spoke to you toward the end of your tour when you were outside the municipal hall?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: That was certainly at the end of our visit to Bijeljina. We had already toured whatever we had to tour, and we were getting ready to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes. And just in relation to that conversation, did she mention an old man to you by the name of Milo Lukic?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, Milo Lukic. He was a brother to a national hero. I believe two persons mentioned to me that he had been killed. She confirmed to me that Milo Lukic, brother of a national hero from World War II - and of course that was at the time the greatest praise one could get, to be called national hero - well his brother, according to her, was killed because he had taken into his home an entire Muslim family to keep them safe. That was how she recounted it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Did she refer to any other killings?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, she was mentioning a cellar where some 22 persons had been killed because a hand grenade had been thrown amongst Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. them. And a boxer, she mentioned a boxer had also having been killed. I don't know who that person was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: What nationality were the people who had been killed?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: As far as I could gather, there were 42 persons killed in all. 27 of them were Muslims, one was a lady Croat, and two were Serbs. I believe one was an elderly man and the other one was Milo Lukic, the brother of the national hero. The lady was an elderly person called Milica. I don't know her last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Omeragic, just for clarification, the numbers that you provided as far as I can quickly add them don't appear to equate. You said 42 persons were killed, 27 were Muslims, one was a Croat and two were Serbs. That's a total of 30 people. Could you again specify --

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: No, 30. 37, I believe, were Bosniaks, Muslims. One lady Croat or a man Croat, I'm not -- actually, I'm not really certain about their nationalities because you know, names tend to be quite similar or unusual. But I believe there were 37 Bosniaks, perhaps two Croats, and then two Serbs or I'm not certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Omeragic. One more matter, did the lady, when she was speaking to you outside the municipal hall, point anyone out to you and give you any information about that person?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: At one point, as I was trying to comfort her, because I was frightened by the colour of her face and I had to react in some way, I was telling her all the time, "Everything is going to be fine." As she was telling me about these murders, she mentioned the name of Jusuf Tanovic. She said that his family had been killed and that his son, perhaps, had also been killed. She pointed to a person that passed by us at a distance of some 60 to 70 metres along a side street as an apparition or a shadow, and she said, "Well that's the person whose family had been killed and he paces the town all day long and cannot find peace."

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: When the lady spoke to you, were other members of the delegation present and if so, who; and how far away from you were they?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: Closest to me was Mr. Fikret Abdic.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I'm trying not to object constantly though there are plenty of opportunities. But just in relation to this, these compound questions, Your Honour, are unacceptable. It's very simple to ask the question and it doesn't require the additional aspects. They can be asked seriatim and it's simply inappropriate because it suggests the answer and it's just not appropriate, Your Honour. The question can be asked very simply: "When the lady spoke to you, who was present?"

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are in the Court's hands on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, on the one hand we are pressing you not to lose any time and also, I do agree with you that it saves quite some time if you put questions in a leading way and of course very often the Defence sees no reason to --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- oppose and that's highly appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I'm trying to use my discretion with these matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: There is a whole series of matters that I could have objected to. I'm not going to. But Your Honour, when we get this sort of compound questions, when it's something that involves this sort of question it really should be led in a more clear-cut fashion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, when I said earlier that -- I'll give you some more guidance once the witness has left in five minutes from now, approximately. That might be more appropriate to do. Until then, you are really in our hands, yes. Could you please reformulate the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Omeragic, when this lady spoke to you, were other members of the delegation present?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: For a while, only -- for the portion of my conversation with the lady, I believe Fikret Abdic was near us and he even joined in at a certain point and said, "Things will work out fine." As soon as the conversation became more serious, we started talking about murders and so on, he turned away and faced the municipality building where other members of the delegation were, Ms. Plavsic and Mr. Prascevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: How far away from Ms. Plavsic and Mr. Prascevic?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: They were some 7 or 8 metres away. Perhaps a bit more, I can't be certain. They were further away and out of earshot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: During the course of your visit to Bijeljina, did you meet a friend of yours who was a reporter from Belgrade and if so, what did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: We met and recognised each other, of course, despite the whole hustle and he was a reporter for Slobodna Bosna as well where I worked.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter missed the name.

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: At one point, as we were talking, I even tried to conceal my true function there and presented myself to him as Abdic's bodyguard and spokesperson and he told me, "Well when did you leave Slobodna Bosna? How come you're not working there any longer?" I continued playing my role because I wanted to conceal the very purpose of my being there. As we were talking, he said, "Everything has been cleaned around here. The streets have been cleared up so that no traces of any fighting remain or traces of anything that would point to what was going on here." He said the streets were cleaned, were washed, that's how he put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I note the time. I just have a very brief video clip which is 30 seconds in duration which I think we could cover in the next five minutes and that is the next exhibit on the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you could do it in three minutes, we could start because I've got one or two observations to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I think we could achieve that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, let's get started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, you may get started and meanwhile, the registrar will think about numbers to be assigned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Omeragic if you could just view your screen and watch this video.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] You will notice the tension, the nervousness in the air.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, if we could just show the witness a clip from that video.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Omeragic, what does that video and this clip depict?

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: It depicts the arrival in front of the Bijeljina municipality building. Should I take people from the left or the right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: If you could indicate to the Court moving from the right of the screen to the left who the people are depicted in that clip.

utterances.speaker: SEAD OMERAGIC
utterances.text: The first person at the right-hand side in jeans and the shirt is me and then a bit up front to the left of me is General Prascevic. The third person from the right is, I believe, Mr. Abdic's driver. The fourth person is Mr. Abdic himself and the fifth person behind in uniform is Predrag Milosavljevic or Vladisavljevic and the sixth person is Mr. Abdic's bodyguard. I believe his name is Mahmutovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Omeragic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, would this be a point to stop. First of all, a very technical matter. The text spoken has not been fully translated for the transcript but I take it that the text was not the most important for you. Ms. Loukas, should we replay that or, if the transcript would be admitted into evidence, the first is an anchorman anyhow and the words according to the transcript spoken, apart from those translated are just: "Indeed, we waited for quite some time for them to arrive for the meeting."

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I don't have a problem with that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then Mr. Registrar, the video would get?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecution Exhibit P585, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 585. Finally we will find out whether there are As or Bs and whether we receive them on CD-ROMs, we'll do that once -- according to our customs and then at least the transcript is P585 and then something added to that, I take it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The video clip is P585, the transcript is P585A, and then English translation will be P585A.1. Yes. Mr. Omeragic, it's already time to stop for the day. We would like to see you back tomorrow morning, 9.00 in this same courtroom. I would like to instruct you not to speak with anyone about your testimony, either testimony already given or still to be given. We'd like to see you back tomorrow. Mr. Usher, could you escort Mr. Omeragic out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two small points at this moment. First of all, we received yesterday the submissions by the Defence on the recall of -- or at least the further cross-examination of Mr. Bjelobrk. Will the OTP respond to that or and if so, when?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I have a chance to look at this evening, I can perhaps respond sometime tomorrow orally if that's acceptable by the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will at least wait for news by tomorrow. That's number one. The second, Mr. Margetts, the issue of leading questions, of course, is extremely difficult because under normal circumstances, you would say no leading questions in chief; on the other hand, if we would follow that system, we'd still be here in 2015.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we put -- our position is that leading questions or wholly appropriate in chief where it's not a contentious matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: So our position is a little different to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course if it's not contentious you would not expect any objection by the other party. That's -- the question now is how to find out whether a matter is contentious or not. First of all, with if we have a statement of course, there could be some communication, you could be -- Ms. Loukas, you could ask specific to Mr. Margetts to, in certain areas, not to lead the witness because you would object. That would be of some guidance for Mr. Margetts, anyhow. At the same time, if I look at the statement, what appears to be the essence of what we at least would expect this testimony is -- of course if we look at a statement, we see that there's quite some information of what happened on the ground. It is the experience of this Chamber that very often, the events that happen on the ground can be put to the witness in a leading way.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And I certainly haven't objected to matters that have sort, Your Honour. I'm adopting a sensible approach in these matters and I'm always happy to give Mr. Margetts guidance. One point that I would make is that it seems to me that -- well, of course this evidence is direct evidence, of course, in relation to Mrs. Plavsic and of course it was a witness that was selected when of course Mrs. Plavsic was co-accused to Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I leave it to you if you want to make any additional observations. But from what I read in this statement, I could imagine that the sensitive issues are first: The knowledge of superior authorities, direct knowledge on what happened on the ground. That might well be a sensitive issue. Perhaps the second issue that might be sensitive is the direct interaction between paramilitaries and people in the superior position in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I would expect objections on leading specifically in those fields, of course, not only because Mrs. Plavsic is a superior -- was a superior authority at least; that's the impression we gained until now. But also that she was in a position for a considerable period of time at least that's our impression as well, on the basis of the evidence we heard until now, that she was in the Presidency together with Mr. Krajisnik. So there, I would expect, as a matter of fact, that sensitivity would lead to objections if you would lead the witness in that respect. If I may make any other comments, since I'm pressing very much to use our time as efficient as possible, I do not know whether the exact formations of the cars and who was sitting next to whom and of course unless you'd like to make a major point out of how at the roadblocks one would pass and what would be authority of a leading politician in getting through the roadblocks. But I didn't get the feeling that that's one of the issues you really wanted to explore. And under those circumstances, you could even wonder whether such questions are at all assisting the Chamber in making the determinations it will have to make. Ms. Loukas, I said I would give you an opportunity to add whatever you wanted.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, fortunately there is no need for me to add anything at this point. The aspects of the guidance that Your Honour has indicated to Mr. Margetts, the areas, of course, that are the areas that must be looked at with some sensitivity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I also can imagine, Mr. Margetts, that the examination-in-chief would then -- apart from dealing with other matters but then perhaps pay more attention to those issues, I mean if they are sensitive for the Defence, they might be of importance for the Prosecution whereas other matters might be covered by other evidence we heard on, I would say crime-base evidence. Not that Bijeljina is not important for crime-base evidence also, but there, for example, one could have thought about -- could have thought about 89(F).

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And in that respect, I'd just like to draw the Court and the Defence's attention to the 92 bis evidence that has been admitted without cross-examination in regard to Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. We would ask ourselves what this evidence, just on main crime base, without any of the other sensitive issues would add to that. But of course it's up to the Prosecution to present its case. With apologies again - I don't want to make that a routine, I hope you understand that - but with apologies to the interpreters and the technicians, we'll adjourn until tomorrow morning, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 13th day of April, 2005, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.53 p.m.
